title: Tissue and therapy assignment in cancers of unknown primary
official: Developing a pipeline for primary tissue assignment and individualised targeted therapy recommendations for cancers of unknown primary
summary:
Background and study aims
Doctors diagnose cancer of unknown primary (CUP) when cancer (primary) has spread to another part of the body (secondary) and doctors can’t tell where it has spread from. Knowing where the cancer started means that better and more effective treatments can be given. The aim of this study is to use samples from secondary tumours from patients to identify what genetic changes have happened in their tumours and use this to work out where the primary site is. We will also use this information to find out what are likely to be the best treatments for each individual patient based on the genetic changes we find in their tumours. We hope that doing both these things will improve the effectiveness of treatments in the future.

Who can participate?
Patients aged 18 years and over who are under the care of clinicians in Sussex-based hospitals who have been diagnosed with a Cancer of Unknown Primary (CUP) or present with a Malignancy of Unknown Origin (MUO). Participants will have undergone, or will already be scheduled to undergo, a biopsy or surgery from which tumour tissue is available. Individuals with hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or HIV are excluded from participation. 

What does the study involve?
Participants will provide consent for researchers to use tumour tissue obtained during routine clinical biopsy or surgery. No additional tissue samples or treatments are required. Tumour samples will undergo genetic sequencing, and the resulting data will be analysed using AI-based prediction tools. 
Researchers will also access relevant information from medical records, including diagnosis, treatment, imaging findings, and outcomes. These data will be anonymised, so the research team will not be able to identify you.
Participation will not affect clinical care, as the software is still under evaluation, but the clinicians will be able to see your results. Participants can request a lay summary of the overall findings to be sent to them once the study is complete.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There are no anticipated physical risks because samples are collected as part of routine clinical care and no additional procedures are required. Participants are unlikely to receive any direct benefit, as study findings will not be used to guide their treatment. However, the research may benefit future patients with CUP by improving diagnosis and treatment approaches.  

Where is the study run from?
The study is coordinated through the University of Sussex, with patients recruited through hospital sites in the University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust and East Sussex NHS Foundation Trust. Samples will be processed through NHS pathology services and sequenced at the Royal Marsden sequencing centre, with data analysis undertaken at the University of Sussex. 

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
June 2026 to May 2028

Who is funding the study?
The study is sponsored by the University of Sussex and funded through a UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) Proof of Concept Grant and PhD studentships from the Sussex Cancer Research Centre and Sussex AI.

Who is the main contact?
Dr Frances Pearl, f.pearl@sussex.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged 18 years or over 
2. Written informed consent according to International Conference on Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) Good Clinical Practice (ICH/GCP) and national regulations
3. ECOG Performance status 0-2
4. Suspected diagnosis of CUP as per the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) guidelines, or presenting with a MOU
5. Well enough for biopsy

Patients must have:
1. The local pathology reports confirming compatibility with CUP diagnosis and the associated slides used for the diagnosis 
2. Discussion at a local CUP Multidisciplinary Team (MDT) suspecting diagnosis 
3. Availability of tumour histological report
Exclusion criteria:
1. Patient with an immunohistochemistry profile that provides a definitive clinical indication of a primary cancer with a specific treatment 
2. Known HIV, Hepatitis B, C positive, due to the difficulties in handling high-risk specimens 
3. Patients who are unable to provide fully informed written consent
